title: Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II Khan Hunting with a Hawk
medium: Oil on paper (as given by arthistoryproject.com); the page calls it a miniature

image.credit: Collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A small, detailed painting of a ruler on horseback holding a hunting hawk on his hand. The horse and rider are the main subject of the picture.

source.museum: Collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: A Mughal-style miniature by Farrukh Beg, dated 1590 to 1595 on the source page, showing Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II riding a horse and holding a hunting hawk. The page tags it Horses and Royalty and says the artist worked as a court painter, including for the Sultan of Bijapur in the Deccan region of India. The page does not name a museum.

descriptions.k: Look at the horse and the rider on its back. The rider holds a bird on his hand. The bird is a hawk. Where is the horse looking? Point to the hawk. What do you think the hawk is about to do?
descriptions.g12: Farrukh Beg painted a ruler riding a horse and holding a hawk. This picture is small, but it has many tiny details. Look closely at the horse, the rider and the bird. Where do you think they are going? Why would someone ride out with a hawk?
descriptions.g35: Farrukh Beg painted this small, detailed picture between 1590 and 1595. It shows Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II on horseback with a hunting hawk. The page calls it a miniature, a kind of small illustration that was often bound into books. Look closely at the horse, the rider and the hawk. What small details show that the painter looked carefully?
descriptions.g68: This Mughal-style miniature by Farrukh Beg shows Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II riding a horse and holding a hunting hawk. The source page says the artist served as a court painter, including for the Sultan of Bijapur, and tags the work Horses and Royalty. How might the painter show that this rider is a ruler? Use the horse, the pose and the details you can see as evidence.
descriptions.g910: Farrukh Beg's miniature (1590 to 1595) shows Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II on horseback with a hunting hawk. A painter trained in the Mughal tradition working for a Deccan court is a sign of how artists and styles moved between courts, though that background is general history and not stated on the work's page. How do the horse, the hawk and the pose build an image of royal power and refinement? Cite details.
descriptions.g1112: Farrukh Beg's miniature (1590 to 1595) presents Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II as a mounted hunter with a hawk, a royal image of mastery over animals. The source page notes that the artist served more than one court, which invites questions about how Mughal visual conventions traveled to the Deccan. How does the picture construct royal identity through horse, hawk and pose, and what might a court portrait leave out? Weigh the visual evidence carefully.

k.daily: Look at the horse and rider. Which one is bigger?
k.emotion: The rider and the hawk look calm and ready. How do you feel when you look at them?
k.observation: Find the hawk. Which part of the rider holds it?
k.analysis: Which is the first thing you look at in this picture, the horse, the rider or the bird?
k.line: Trace the shape of the horse's back and neck with your finger. Is the line curvy or straight?
k.shape: Look at the horse's legs and the hawk's wings. What shapes do you see in them?
k.color: Point to your favorite color in the picture. Where else do you see it?
k.texture: Imagine petting the horse and touching the hawk's feathers. How would each one feel?
k.space: The picture is very small. What can you find close to the horse?
k.light: Look for the lightest spot in the picture. What is it on?
k.meaning: Why might a ruler want a picture of himself on a horse?
k.culture: Long ago, some people hunted with trained birds. What do you think a hawk needed to learn?
k.technique: This painting is small, so the painter used tiny brushes. Find the smallest detail you can see.
k.personal: If you could ride the horse, where would you go?
k.critical: What would you change if you painted this horse and rider yourself?

g12.daily: Why do you think the painter chose to show a rider with a hawk and not just a horse?
g12.emotion: What mood does the rider's pose give the picture, calm, proud or excited?
g12.observation: List five things you can find on the horse and the rider.
g12.analysis: How does the painter make you look at the rider first?
g12.line: Follow the outline of the horse from head to tail. Where does the line curve the most?
g12.shape: Which shapes make up the horse, and which shapes make up the hawk?
g12.color: Which colors did the painter use for the horse and the rider, and how do they stand out?
g12.texture: How did the painter show the difference between the horse's coat and the rider's clothing?
g12.space: Where do the horse's legs and the ground meet, and what does that tell you about where the horse stands?
g12.light: Which parts of the picture look brightest, and why might the painter have chosen them?
g12.meaning: What do the horse and the hawk tell you about the person riding?
g12.culture: This picture was painted for a royal court long ago. What does it show you about how a ruler wanted to be seen?
g12.technique: Why do you think the painter worked so carefully on such a small picture?
g12.personal: What animal would you like to ride or work with, and why?
g12.critical: How would the picture feel different if the rider were walking and not riding?

g35.daily: What small details in the horse, the rider or the hawk show how closely the painter looked?
g35.emotion: What feeling does the rider's calm hold on the hawk create, and what details support your idea?
g35.observation: Describe the pose of the rider's arm and the position of the hawk. What do you notice?
g35.analysis: How does the painter arrange the horse, rider and hawk so each can be seen clearly?
g35.line: How do the curved lines of the horse's body and the rider's clothing add movement or calm?
g35.shape: What shapes do the horse and the hawk make, and how do they fit together as one group?
g35.color: How do the colors make the rider and the horse stand out from what is around them?
g35.texture: What different textures, such as fur, feathers and cloth, can you find, and how did the painter suggest them?
g35.space: How does the painter show that the horse is in a place and not floating on the page?
g35.light: Where is the light strongest in the picture, and what does it make you notice?
g35.meaning: The page tags this picture Royalty. What details might tell us the rider is an important person?
g35.culture: What can this picture tell us about the things a royal court enjoyed, such as horses and hunting with birds?
g35.technique: A miniature is a small, detailed picture. What skills would a painter need to work at this size?
g35.personal: What would you want to ask the rider if you could talk to him?
g35.critical: How is a painted picture of a ruler different from a photograph of a person today?

g68.daily: Which details in this miniature make it feel like a portrait of a ruler and not only a picture of a rider?
g68.emotion: How do the poise of the rider and the steadiness of the hawk shape the mood of the image?
g68.observation: Compare how the painter shows the horse's body with how the painter shows the rider's clothing and the hawk. What do you notice?
g68.analysis: How does the arrangement of horse, rider and hawk guide your eye through such a small picture?
g68.line: How do the contours of the horse and the rider's figure create rhythm or movement across the page?
g68.shape: How do the large forms of the horse contrast with the small, sharp forms of the hawk?
g68.color: How does the choice of colors help separate the figures from their setting and show their importance?
g68.texture: How does the painter suggest different surfaces, such as a coat, feathers and fabric, in a very small space?
g68.space: How does the painter handle depth in a small miniature, and what clues tell you where the figures stand?
g68.light: How does the distribution of light and dark direct attention to the rider and the hawk?
g68.meaning: The hawk and horse are both signs of a hunt. What might they say about the rider's role and interests?
g68.culture: How might a painting like this have been used or seen at a royal court, and who might have looked at it?
g68.technique: What does the fine, careful finish of this miniature show about the training and patience of the painter?
g68.personal: What would you choose to include in a portrait of yourself to show who you are?
g68.critical: How reliable is a court painting as evidence about a real person? Use details from the image in your answer.

g910.daily: How do the horse, the hawk and the pose work together to shape the viewer's impression of the sultan?
g910.emotion: What tone, formal, relaxed or alert, does the figure's bearing establish, and which details create it?
g910.observation: Examine the points where the hawk, the hand and the horse meet. What do they reveal about the painter's attention to detail?
g910.analysis: How does the composition give the rider authority while still making room for the animals?
g910.line: How does linear contour in this miniature define the forms of horse, rider and bird, and how does it contribute to elegance?
g910.shape: How do the large mass of the horse and the compact form of the hawk balance each other in the composition?
g910.color: How does the use of color separate figure from ground and support the sense of a refined court image?
g910.texture: How does the painter distinguish animal, human and fabric surfaces within a small format?
g910.space: How does the miniature format and its handling of space compare with the way a large oil painting might present a rider?
g910.light: What role does light play in modeling the figures, and is it naturalistic or decorative?
g910.meaning: How does the pairing of horse and hawk communicate ideas of skill, leisure and rule?
g910.culture: How does a Mughal-trained painter working at the Bijapur court illustrate the movement of artistic ideas between courts? Note which parts are general history.
g910.technique: What does the choice of a small, detailed format tell you about how and where the work was meant to be viewed?
g910.personal: How do you present yourself in pictures, and how is that similar to or different from how a ruler chose to appear?
g910.critical: To what extent can a flattering royal image also be reliable evidence about the person it shows?

g1112.daily: How does the image turn a hunting scene into a statement of royal identity, and what does it leave unsaid?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the composure of rider and hawk support a reading of controlled power and refinement?
g1112.observation: Scan the finest passages of the miniature. What do they suggest about the painter's priorities and the viewing conditions for which it was made?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional hierarchy of rider, horse and hawk construct a particular idea of mastery?
g1112.line: How might the quality of contour in this miniature connect to a courtly ideal of precision, and where does it depart from naturalism?
g1112.shape: How do the interplay of large and small forms, mount and bird, set up a relationship between strength and finesse?
g1112.color: How does color function here, as description, as ornament or as a sign of status, and how would you test each possibility?
g1112.texture: How does the painter's rendering of varied surfaces within a small format reflect a studio tradition of technical training?
g1112.space: How does the miniature's handling of space shape the viewer's relationship to the figure, intimate or distant?
g1112.light: How does the treatment of light, whether descriptive or ornamental, relate to the conventions of court painting?
g1112.meaning: The page tags the work Horses and Royalty. How might those two themes reinforce each other, and what other readings are possible?
g1112.culture: The source page says the artist served more than one court. How might that mobility complicate a single label such as Mughal painting?
g1112.technique: How do the medium given by the site, oil on paper, and the small format shape what the painter could achieve here?
g1112.personal: How does your own sense of how a leader should look and act shape the way you meet this image?
g1112.critical: What would a persuasive argument look like that this work is propaganda as much as portrait, and what visual evidence would you need?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, year range (1590-1595; image file name says 1595), medium (oil on paper, as the site gives it), movement (Mughal), tags (Horses, Royalty) and the public-domain statement were read from the arthistoryproject.com page text. The page does not name a collection. Subject is a ruler on horseback with a hunting hawk; no violence, nudity or other sensitive content was identified from the text, but a hunt could in principle show animals being hunted. The Bijapur court context and that a Mughal-trained painter worked there is general art history supplemented by the page's note that the artist served the Sultan of Bijapur. The altText and descriptions avoid colours and details not supported by the text. The image file has not been viewed; a person should view it and confirm it before release.

teacherNote.context: A small Mughal-style painting by Farrukh Beg, dated 1590 to 1595, of Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II on horseback holding a hunting hawk. The source page does not name a museum, and it gives the medium as oil on paper.
directions: Have younger students draw a rider and an animal companion, adding as many small details as they can, then explain what the animal does.
Ask older students to list visual clues that signal status (horse, hawk, pose) and compare them with how leaders are shown in photographs today.
Discuss how an artist can move between courts and how a style can change when it travels. Note which points come from the page and which are general history.
